claim: T-cell acute lymphoblastic leukemia (T-ALL) represents approximately 10–15% of pediatric cases of all acute lymphoblastic leukemia.
source: Representing approximately 10–15% of pediatric cases and 25% of adult cases of all acute lymphoblastic leukemia (Vadillo et al., 2018), T-ALL originates in the thymus.
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Vadillo et al., 2018, which provides the statistical data.

claim: T-cell acute lymphoblastic leukemia (T-ALL) represents 25% of adult cases of all acute lymphoblastic leukemia.
source: Representing approximately 10–15% of pediatric cases and 25% of adult cases of all acute lymphoblastic leukemia (Vadillo et al., 2018), T-ALL originates in the thymus.
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Vadillo et al., 2018, which provides the statistical data.

claim: T-ALL originates in the thymus.
source: Representing approximately 10–15% of pediatric cases and 25% of adult cases of all acute lymphoblastic leukemia (Vadillo et al., 2018), T-ALL originates in the thymus.
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Vadillo et al., 2018.

claim: Over 50% of T-ALL patients harbor gain-of-function mutations in the NOTCH1 gene.
source: Notably, over 50% of T-ALL patients harbor gain-of-function mutations in the NOTCH1 gene, which encodes the receptor for DLL4, while around 10% of patients exhibit similar mutations in the IL-7 receptor (IL7R) gene (Liu et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Liu et al., 2017, which provides the statistical data on NOTCH1 mutations in T-ALL patients.

claim: Around 10% of T-ALL patients exhibit gain-of-function mutations in the IL-7 receptor (IL7R) gene.
source: Notably, over 50% of T-ALL patients harbor gain-of-function mutations in the NOTCH1 gene, which encodes the receptor for DLL4, while around 10% of patients exhibit similar mutations in the IL-7 receptor (IL7R) gene (Liu et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Liu et al., 2017, which provides the statistical data on IL7R mutations in T-ALL patients.

claim: The NOTCH1 gene encodes the receptor for DLL4.
source: Notably, over 50% of T-ALL patients harbor gain-of-function mutations in the NOTCH1 gene, which encodes the receptor for DLL4, while around 10% of patients exhibit similar mutations in the IL-7 receptor (IL7R) gene (Liu et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by established scientific knowledge and is stated in the context of a citation to Liu et al., 2017.

claim: The leukemogenic potential of constitutive activation of NOTCH1 and IL7R receptors has been demonstrated across various vertebrate models.
source: The leukemogenic potential of constitutive activation of these receptors has been demonstrated across various vertebrate models (González-García et al., 2009; Silva et al., 2021; Shochat et al., 2011; Zenatti et al., 2011; Oliveira et al., 2022; Chen et al., 2007; Blackburn et al., 2012), emphasizing the evolutionary conservation of thymic developmental mechanisms that become misrouted in T-ALL (Bajoghli et al., 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations to studies demonstrating leukemogenic potential in various vertebrate models.

claim: Thymic developmental mechanisms that become misrouted in T-ALL are evolutionarily conserved.
source: The leukemogenic potential of constitutive activation of these receptors has been demonstrated across various vertebrate models (González-García et al., 2009; Silva et al., 2021; Shochat et al., 2011; Zenatti et al., 2011; Oliveira et al., 2022; Chen et al., 2007; Blackburn et al., 2012), emphasizing the evolutionary conservation of thymic developmental mechanisms that become misrouted in T-ALL (Bajoghli et al., 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Bajoghli et al., 2019, which discusses the evolutionary conservation of thymic developmental mechanisms.

claim: The virtual thymus model simulates individual thymocytes using agents within a spatially resolved 'virtual thymus' to explore cell-level behaviors and their effects on thymocyte population dynamics.
source: Our recently developed cell-based computational model, for example, simulates individual thymocytes using agents within a spatially resolved 'virtual thymus' to explore cell-level behaviors and their effects on thymocyte population dynamics.
evidence: The claim describes the methodology of the virtual thymus model developed by the authors.

claim: The virtual thymus model was originally developed to investigate the impact of thymic niche signals and intrathymic cell localization on the αβ/γδ T-cell sublineage outcomes.
source: This model was originally developed to investigate the impact of thymic niche signals and intrathymic cell localization on the αβ/γδ T-cell sublineage outcomes (Aghaallaei et al., 2021).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Aghaallaei et al., 2021, which describes the original purpose of the model.

claim: The computational representation of the virtual thymus focuses on a 5 µm deep slice of the lower half of the radially symmetric organ, approximately 1/10 of the total volume of a medaka embryonic thymus.
source: To reduce computational cost, the computational representation focuses on a 5 µm deep slice of the lower half of the radially symmetric organ, approximately 1/10 of the total volume of a medaka embryonic thymus (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A and B).
evidence: The claim is supported by the text description and reference to Figure 1—figure supplement 1A and B, which provides visual evidence.

claim: In the virtual thymus model, each simulation step represents 15 seconds.
source: For time calibration, each simulation step was set to represent 15 s.
evidence: The claim describes a parameter setting in the computational model.

claim: With a total of 48,000 steps per simulation, the entire simulation spans 720,000 seconds, equivalent to about 8.3 days.
source: With a total of 48,000 steps per simulation, the entire simulation spans 720,000 s, equivalent to about 8.3 days (Figure 1D).
evidence: The claim is supported by the text description and reference to Figure 1D, which provides visual evidence of the timeline.

claim: Each simulation starts with entering the first ETP into the virtual thymus and ends with a homeostatic cell population of roughly 100 cells.
source: Correspondingly, each simulation starts with entering the first ETP into the virtual thymus and ends with a homeostatic cell population of roughly 100 cells (mean ± standard deviation: 98±7; Figure 1—video 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by the text description and reference to Figure 1—video 1, which provides visual evidence.

claim: At 11 dpf, the medaka thymus contains 877±146 (N=7) thymocytes.
source: At 11 dpf, the medaka thymus contains 877±146 (N=7) thymocytes.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from medaka fish.

claim: The cell population in the virtual thymus model reproduces the temporal dynamics in medaka within the margin of error.
source: Considering that the virtual thymus represents 1/10 of the medaka embryonic thymus, the cell population in the virtual thymus model reproduces the temporal dynamics in medaka within the margin of error.
evidence: The claim is based on a comparison between the virtual model and experimental data from medaka.

claim: All virtual TECs in the model express Dll4.
source: Consistent with medaka WT embryonic thymus (Aghaallaei et al., 2021; Aghaallaei et al., 2022), all virtual TECs in this model express the Dll4 (Figure 1E, top-right panel), with a subset spatially releasing IL-7 into the environment (Figure 1E, top-left panel), creating a short-ranged IL-7 cytokine gradient in the thymic cortex niche (Aghaallaei et al., 2021).
evidence: The claim is supported by the text description and reference to Figure 1E, which shows Dll4 expression in TECs.

claim: A subset of virtual TECs spatially release IL-7 into the environment, creating a short-ranged IL-7 cytokine gradient in the thymic cortex niche.
source: Consistent with medaka WT embryonic thymus (Aghaallaei et al., 2021; Aghaallaei et al., 2022), all virtual TECs in this model express the Dll4 (Figure 1E, top-right panel), with a subset spatially releasing IL-7 into the environment (Figure 1E, top-left panel), creating a short-ranged IL-7 cytokine gradient in the thymic cortex niche (Aghaallaei et al., 2021).
evidence: The claim is supported by the text description and reference to Figure 1E, which shows IL-7 distribution in the virtual thymus.

claim: All ETPs uniformly express the Notch1 receptor.
source: In terms of cell-intrinsic factors, all ETPs uniformly express the Notch1 receptor (Figure 1E, middle-right panel), and each cell lineage expresses the IL-7 receptor (IL7R) at a constant level chosen randomly between 0 and 1 (Figure 1E, middle-left panel).
evidence: The claim is supported by the text description and reference to Figure 1E, which shows Notch1 expression in ETPs.

claim: Each cell lineage expresses the IL-7 receptor (IL7R) at a constant level chosen randomly between 0 and 1.
source: In terms of cell-intrinsic factors, all ETPs uniformly express the Notch1 receptor (Figure 1E, middle-right panel), and each cell lineage expresses the IL-7 receptor (IL7R) at a constant level chosen randomly between 0 and 1 (Figure 1E, middle-left panel).
evidence: The claim is supported by the text description and reference to Figure 1E, which shows IL7R expression in thymocytes.

claim: The cell cycle was modeled with an average duration of 7 hours and was subdivided into G1, S, G2, and M phases.
source: The cell cycle was modeled with an average duration of 7 hr and was subdivided into G1, S, G2, and M phases.
evidence: The claim describes a parameter setting in the computational model.

claim: Virtual cells require external pro-proliferative signals during the G1 phase to commit to S through M.
source: In line with in vivo observations (Ruijtenberg and van den Heuvel, 2016), virtual cells require external pro-proliferative signals during the G1 phase to commit to S through M.
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Ruijtenberg and van den Heuvel, 2016, which describes in vivo observations.

claim: Once differentiated, cells can no longer enter the cell cycle.
source: Once differentiated, cells can no longer enter the cell cycle.
evidence: The claim describes a rule in the computational model.

claim: The dynamics of pro-proliferative signals and the proliferation stop after differentiation allow clones in silico to undergo up to 4 rounds of cell division.
source: The dynamics of pro-proliferative signals and the proliferation stop after differentiation allow clones in silico to undergo up to 4 rounds of cell division (Aghaallaei et al., 2021).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Aghaallaei et al., 2021, which describes the model behavior.

claim: Thymic selection is modeled as a probabilistic event and is not regulated by signaling dynamics.
source: Thymic selection is modeled as a probabilistic event and is not regulated by signaling dynamics.
evidence: The claim describes a modeling choice in the computational model.

claim: Using confocal imaging, the relative area occupied by thymocytes was estimated at 53 ± 3% (N=4) and TECs at 47 ± 3% (N=4).
source: Using confocal imaging, we estimated the relative area occupied by thymocytes (53 ± 3%; N=4) and TECs (47 ± 3%; N=4).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from confocal imaging.

claim: In the in silico model, thymocytes take up on average 56±2% and TECs 44±2% of the volume in homeostasis.
source: A similar morphology and tissue density was replicated in our in silico model (Figure 2A, right panel), with thymocytes taking up on average 56±2% and TECs 44±2% of the volume in homeostasis.
evidence: The claim is supported by the text description and reference to Figure 2A, which shows the in silico model.

claim: A higher density of larger TECs with more protrusions led to an almost twofold increase in the number of thymocytes (200±13, N=3; scenario 26) compared to the reference condition (98±7, N=19).
source: The results from 26 different tested conditions predicted that a higher density of larger TECs with more protrusions led to an almost twofold increase in the number of thymocytes (200±13, N=3; scenario 26 in Figure 2C, Figure 2—figure supplement 1A, bottom) compared to the reference condition (98±7, N=19; reference in Figure 2C).
evidence: The claim is supported by the text description and reference to Figure 2C, which shows the simulation results.

claim: Scenarios where TEC size, number of protrusions, and density were reduced diminished the homeostatic thymocyte population size.
source: Conversely, scenarios where these parameters were reduced, particularly a reduced TEC size, also diminished the homeostatic thymocyte population size (scenarios 1–14 in Figure 2C).
evidence: The claim is supported by the text description and reference to Figure 2C, which shows the simulation results.

claim: In scenario 1, with a reduced TEC size but unchanged number of protrusions and density, the thymocyte population size was 45±1 (N=3).
source: The condition with the least amount of cells, scenario 1, had a reduced TEC size, but an unchanged number of protrusions and density. The condition diametrically opposite to scenario 26 was scenario 6, with a reduced TEC size, reduced number of protrusions, and reduced TEC density (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A, top). In both scenario 1 (45±1, N=3) and scenario 6 (51±2, N=3), the thymic population size was only about half of that in the reference condition (98∓7, N=19).
evidence: The claim is supported by the text description and reference to Figure 2—figure supplement 1A, which shows the simulation results.

claim: In scenario 6, with a reduced TEC size, reduced number of protrusions, and reduced TEC density, the thymocyte population size was 51±2 (N=3).
source: The condition with the least amount of cells, scenario 1, had a reduced TEC size, but an unchanged number of protrusions and density. The condition diametrically opposite to scenario 26 was scenario 6, with a reduced TEC size, reduced number of protrusions, and reduced TEC density (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A, top). In both scenario 1 (45±1, N=3) and scenario 6 (51±2, N=3), the thymic population size was only about half of that in the reference condition (98∓7, N=19).
evidence: The claim is supported by the text description and reference to Figure 2—figure supplement 1A, which shows the simulation results.

claim: Statistical analysis confirmed that all three parameters (TEC size, number of protrusions, and density) and their interactions were significant predictors of total thymocyte population size.
source: Statistical analysis confirmed that all three parameters and their interactions were significant predictors of total thymocyte population size (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B and C).
evidence: The claim is supported by the text description and reference to Figure 2—figure supplement 1B and C, which shows the statistical analysis results.

claim: The statistically significant interaction between TEC parameters can be explained by the fact that higher TEC density increases the number of TECs and thereby amplifies the effect of an increased TEC radius or number of protrusions.
source: The statistically significant interaction can be explained by the fact that higher TEC density increases the number of TECs and thereby amplifies the effect of an increased TEC radius or number of protrusions.
evidence: The claim is based on an inference from the statistical analysis results.

claim: These three alterations of the thymic niche morphology act synergistically to modulate thymocyte population size.
source: Thus, these three alterations of the thymic niche morphology act synergistically to modulate thymocyte population size.
evidence: The claim is based on an inference from the simulation results and statistical analysis.

claim: In scenario 27, where all TECs express IL-7, the extracellular level of IL-7 and thymocyte population size (155±11, N=5) was similarly high as in scenario 26.
source: In scenario 27, TECs maintained their reference architecture and density but all expressed IL-7, leading to a more uniform cytokine distribution in the thymic environment (Figure 2E). The extracellular level of IL-7 (Figure 2F) and thymocyte population size (155±11, N=5; Figure 2G) in scenario 27 was similarly high as in scenario 26, where the size, protrusion number, and density of TECs were increased.
evidence: The claim is supported by the text description and reference to Figures 2E, 2F, and 2G, which show the simulation results.

claim: When TECs did not express IL-7 (scenario 28), the thymocyte population size (42±1, N=5) was low, akin to scenario 6.
source: Conversely, when TECs did not express IL-7 (scenario 28), the thymocyte population size (Figure 2G) was low (42±1, N=5), akin to scenario 6, where the size, protrusion, and density of TECs were reduced.
evidence: The claim is supported by the text description and reference to Figure 2G, which shows the simulation results.

claim: Although the average extracellular IL-7 level is at its highest in scenario 27 with ubiquitous expression, the spatially restricted elevated IL-7 concentration in scenario 26 is more effective at driving thymic population growth.
source: Interestingly, although the average extracellular IL-7 level is at its highest in scenario 27 with ubiquitous expression, the spatially restricted elevated IL-7 concentration in scenario 26 is more effective at driving thymic population growth (Figure 2E–G).
evidence: The claim is supported by the text description and reference to Figures 2E–G, which show the simulation results.

claim: Thymocytes first enter the organ at its periphery from below (at the ventrolateral site), where IL-7 levels are highest, and tend to migrate to the IL-7-depleted center of the thymus as they become non-proliferative.
source: Thymocytes first enter the organ at its periphery from below (at the ventrolateral site), where IL-7 levels are highest, and tend to migrate to the IL-7-depleted center of the thymus as they become non-proliferative (Aghaallaei et al., 2021; see also Figure 1—video 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Aghaallaei et al., 2021, and reference to Figure 1—video 1, which shows the migration pattern.

claim: In scenario 26, thymocytes in their proliferative phase immediately encounter elevated IL-7 at the organ periphery, stimulating cell proliferation.
source: Thus, in scenario 26, thymocytes in their proliferative phase immediately encounter elevated IL-7 at the organ periphery, stimulating cell proliferation.
evidence: The claim is based on an inference from the simulation results and the spatial distribution of IL-7.

claim: In scenario 27, thymocytes that enter the organ periphery encounter comparable levels of IL-7 to the reference scenario, and only after entering deeper into the organ can the ubiquitous expression of IL-7 unfold its effects.
source: In contrast, in scenario 27, thymocytes that enter the organ periphery encounter comparable levels of IL-7 to the reference scenario, and only after entering deeper into the organ can the ubiquitous expression of IL-7 unfold its effects.
evidence: The claim is based on an inference from the simulation results and the spatial distribution of IL-7.

claim: The delay in IL-7 exposure in scenario 27, contingent to random cell migration (which is further exacerbated by cell crowding posing an obstacle), reduces the impact of elevated IL-7.
source: This delay, contingent to random cell migration (which is further exacerbated by cell crowding posing an obstacle), reduces the impact of elevated IL-7 in scenario 27.
evidence: The claim is based on an inference from the simulation results and the spatial distribution of IL-7.

claim: The spatial structure of the thymic niche can impact thymocyte population dynamics.
source: These results highlight how the spatial structure of the thymic niche can impact thymocyte population dynamics.
evidence: The claim is based on an inference from the simulation results.

claim: il7 crispant embryos displayed fewer thymocytes and a smaller thymus size.
source: Consistent with our in silico outcomes, il7 crispant embryos displayed fewer thymocytes and a smaller thymus size (Figure 2I, Figure 2—figure supplement 2C and D).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from il7 crispant embryos and reference to Figures 2I and 2—figure supplement 2C and D.

claim: A reduction in IL-7 availability in the thymus reduces thymocyte proliferation.
source: To estimate the extent of cell proliferation, we counted mitotic cells throughout the entire thymus using the M phase marker phospho-histone 3 (pH3) and normalized values to the mean of the control. This analysis further supported that a reduction in IL-7 availability in the thymus reduces thymocyte proliferation (Figure 2I and J).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from pH3 staining and reference to Figures 2I and J.

claim: The thymus of TEC:IL-7HI embryos appeared visibly larger, and the number of pH3 positive cells was significantly increased compared to WT.
source: Compared to WT, the thymus of TEC:IL-7HI embryos appeared visibly larger, and the number of pH3 positive cells was significantly increased (Figure 2I and J).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from TEC:IL-7HI embryos and reference to Figures 2I and J.

claim: The in vivo results confirm the critical role of IL-7 for thymocyte proliferation in medaka, a mechanism that is evolutionarily conserved among vertebrates.
source: Therefore, the in vivo results confirm the critical role of IL-7 for thymocyte proliferation in medaka, a mechanism that is evolutionarily conserved among vertebrates (Iwanami et al., 2011).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data and a citation to Iwanami et al., 2011, which discusses the evolutionary conservation of IL-7's role.

claim: The alterations in thymic size suggest a regulatory crosstalk between thymocyte proliferation and TEC architecture.
source: Additionally, the alterations in thymic size suggest a regulatory crosstalk between thymocyte proliferation and TEC architecture.
evidence: The claim is based on an inference from the experimental observations of thymic size changes.

claim: The scenario with the highest number of thymocytes occurred when signaling deactivation was low and activation was high (274±11, N=4; scenario 45).
source: Indeed, the scenario with the highest number of thymocytes occurred when signaling deactivation was low and activation was high (274±11, N=4; scenario 45 in Figure 3C).
evidence: The claim is supported by the text description and reference to Figure 3C, which shows the simulation results.

claim: The diametrically opposite combination of signaling parameters had the least amount of cells (42±1, N=4; scenario 29).
source: The diametrically opposite combination had the least amount of cells (42±1, N=4; scenario 29 in Figure 3C).
evidence: The claim is supported by the text description and reference to Figure 3C, which shows the simulation results.

claim: Statistical analysis confirms that signal transduction activation aIL-7 and the signal transduction deactivation rate dIL-7 were both statistically significant predictors of thymocyte population size.
source: Statistical analysis confirms that signal transduction activation aIL-7 and the signal transduction deactivation rate dIL-7 were both statistically significant predictors of thymocyte population size (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by the text description and reference to Figure 3—figure supplement 1, which shows the statistical analysis results.

claim: There was only a limited reduction in population size with IL-7 depletion (91±11, N=4; scenario 36) compared to no depletion in the reference setting (98±7, N=19).
source: There was only a limited reduction in population size with IL-7 depletion (91±11, N=4; scenario 36 in Figure 3C) compared to no depletion in our reference setting (98±7, N=19).
evidence: The claim is supported by the text description and reference to Figure 3C, which shows the simulation results.

claim: Overall, IL-7 depletion did not have a significant effect on thymocyte population.
source: Overall, IL-7 depletion did not have a significant effect on thymocyte population (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by the text description and reference to Figure 3—figure supplement 1, which shows the statistical analysis results.

claim: Population size difference due to IL-7 depletion was more pronounced at higher cell numbers, e.g., comparing between scenario 44 (237±7, N=4) and scenario 45 (274±11, N=4).
source: However, we noted that population size difference was more pronounced at higher cell numbers, e.g., comparing between scenario 44 (237±7, N=4) and scenario 45 (274±11, N=4).
evidence: The claim is supported by the text description of the simulation results.

claim: Thymocyte proliferation could self-inhibit via depletion of extracellular IL-7, but this effect is expected to be small unless cell numbers are massively increased.
source: Therefore, thymocyte proliferation could self-inhibit via depletion of extracellular IL-7, but we expect this effect to be small unless cell numbers are massively increased.
evidence: The claim is based on an inference from the simulation results.

claim: Introducing a lesioned clone did not markedly alter the division behavior of non-lesioned clones in the same simulation.
source: The clonal analysis of simulations revealed that introducing a lesioned clone did not markedly alter the division behavior of non-lesioned clones in the same simulation (scenario with no lesion: 1.04±1.26 rounds of cell division; scenario with IL7RDA: 0.98±1.22 rounds of cell division; scenario with IL7RHI: 1.04±1.23 rounds of cell division; Figure 4B and C).
evidence: The claim is supported by the text description and reference to Figures 4B and C, which show the simulation results.

claim: Lesioned clones averaged just above 4 rounds of cell division (4.20±0.34 for IL7RDA and 4.10±0.13 for IL7RHI).
source: In contrast, lesioned clones averaged just above 4 rounds of cell division (4.20±0.34 for IL7RDA and 4.10±0.13 for IL7RHI).
evidence: The claim is supported by the text description of the simulation results.

claim: The size of IL7RDA and IL7RHI clones was nearly eightfold larger than an average non-lesioned clone.
source: Consequently, the size of IL7RDA and IL7RHI clones was nearly eightfold larger than an average non-lesioned clone (Figure 4C).
evidence: The claim is supported by the text description and reference to Figure 4C, which shows the simulation results.

claim: Lesioned clones acquired a distinct proliferative advantage over non-lesioned clones in the virtual thymus model.
source: This result suggests that lesioned clones acquired a distinct proliferative advantage over non-lesioned clones in our virtual thymus model.
evidence: The claim is based on an inference from the simulation results.

claim: The virtual thymus model predicts that a single lesion in the IL7R gene will not be clinically impactful.
source: Nevertheless, since the expansion of lesioned clones amounted to, at best, only one additional round of cell division compared to the upper range of the non-lesioned clone distribution (Figure 4C), our virtual thymus model predicts that a single lesion in the IL7R gene will not be clinically impactful.
evidence: The claim is based on an inference from the simulation results.

claim: Certain malignant T cells derived from T-ALL patients possess the ability to ectopically express IL-7 cytokine.
source: The inclusion of the latter was inspired by a study showing that certain malignant T cells derived from T-ALL patients possess the ability to ectopically express IL-7 cytokine (Buffière et al., 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Buffière et al., 2019, which describes ectopic IL-7 expression in malignant T cells.

claim: 1580 scenarios were simulated in the systematic approach.
source: In the end, 1580 scenarios were simulated.
evidence: The claim describes the number of scenarios simulated in the study.

claim: Overall, a similar proliferation pattern was observed among IL7RHI and IL7RDA clones in most of the tested scenarios.
source: Overall, we observed a similar proliferation pattern among IL7RHI and IL7RDA clones in most of the tested scenarios.
evidence: The claim is based on an observation from the simulation results.

claim: Non-lesioned clones displayed similar trends as clones in control simulations that lacked a lesioned clone.
source: Likewise, non-lesioned clones displayed similar trends as clones in control simulations that lacked a lesioned clone (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by the text description and reference to Figure 4—figure supplement 1, which shows the simulation results.

claim: The lesioned clones consistently showed a higher proliferation rate than their non-lesioned counterpart.
source: The lesioned clones consistently showed a higher proliferation rate than their non-lesioned counterpart (Figure 4E; Figure 4—source data 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by the text description and reference to Figure 4E and Figure 4—source data 1, which show the simulation results.

claim: Lesioned clones disproportionally gained up to 6 rounds of cell division by modulating proliferative parameters, while normal clones only gained 2 rounds of cell division in the same scenarios.
source: In fact, lesioned clones disproportionally gained up to 6 rounds of cell division by modulating proliferative parameters, while normal clones only gained 2 rounds of cell division in the same scenarios.
evidence: The claim is supported by the text description of the simulation results.

claim: In the scenario with increased proliferation, the first clones to colonize the organ can massively proliferate and completely surround the TECs, preventing later arriving clones from accessing TEC-derived pro-proliferative signals.
source: This difference results from cell crowding creating a disproportional disadvantage to non-lesioned clones: In the scenario with increased proliferation, the first clones to colonize the organ can massively proliferate and completely surround the TECs, preventing later arriving clones from accessing TEC-derived pro-proliferative signals (Figure 4—video 2, right column).
evidence: The claim is based on an inference from the simulation results and reference to Figure 4—video 2.

claim: Lesioned clones carry an intrinsic pro-proliferative advantage due to their lesions in the IL7R, enabling proliferation despite a lack of direct contact with TECs.
source: Thus, these few 'lucky' early colonizers prevent late cells from attaining their full proliferative potential. Lesioned clones carry an intrinsic pro-proliferative advantage due to their lesions in the IL7R, enabling proliferation despite a lack of direct contact with TECs.
evidence: The claim is based on an inference from the simulation results.

claim: Modifying parameters that affected IL-7 activity only enhanced the proliferation rate of non-lesioned clones but showed no impact on either IL7RHI or IL7RDA clones.
source: In contrast, modifying parameters that affected IL-7 activity only enhanced the proliferation rate of non-lesioned clones but showed no impact on either IL7RHI or IL7RDA clones (Figure 4—figure supplement 3).
evidence: The claim is supported by the text description and reference to Figure 4—figure supplement 3, which shows the simulation results.

claim: For IL7RHI clones, 10-fold receptor overexpression is enough to activate downstream pro-proliferative effects of the pathway regardless of the parameter permutations tested.
source: While this outcome is expected for IL7RDA clones, which are insensitive to IL-7, for IL7RHI clones, it indicates that 10-fold receptor overexpression is enough to activate downstream pro-proliferative effects of the pathway regardless of the parameter permutations that we tested.
evidence: The claim is based on an inference from the simulation results.

claim: Proliferation of normal clones is strongly affected by IL-7 signaling parameters, gaining up to 3 rounds of cell division between least and most proliferative conditions.
source: In contrast, proliferation of normal clones is strongly affected in these conditions, gaining up to 3 rounds of cell division between least and most proliferative conditions.
evidence: The claim is supported by the text description of the simulation results.

claim: No added effect on clonal expansion was detected from combining reduced cell motility or autocrine IL-7 production with IL7RHI or IL7RDA lesions.
source: In our systematic approach, we did not detect an added effect on clonal expansion from combining reduced cell motility or autocrine IL-7 production with IL7RHI or IL7RDA lesions (Figure 4—figure supplement 4).
evidence: The claim is supported by the text description and reference to Figure 4—figure supplement 4, which shows the simulation results.

claim: Added IL-7 secretion by lesioned clones with the autocrine lesion had only a small effect on proliferation of non-lesioned clones in the same simulation.
source: Added IL-7 secretion by lesioned clones with the autocrine lesion had only a small effect on proliferation of non-lesioned clones in the same simulation.
evidence: The claim is supported by the text description of the simulation results.

claim: The most critical lesion in conferring a proliferative advantage to lesioned clones was a delay in differentiation.
source: The most critical lesion in conferring a proliferative advantage to lesioned clones was a delay in differentiation.
evidence: The claim is based on an observation from the simulation results.

claim: A delay in differentiation essentially doubled the duration of the proliferative phase, and indeed up to 8 rounds of cell division were observed, double the level of clones having only a single lesion in the IL7R.
source: This delay essentially doubled the duration of the proliferative phase, and indeed we observed up to 8 rounds of cell division, double the level of clones having only a single lesion in the IL7R.
evidence: The claim is supported by the text description of the simulation results.

claim: Perturbations in differentiation have been implicated in contributing to the initiation and progression of cancer.
source: This result fits well with in vivo data, suggesting that perturbations in differentiation have been implicated in contributing to the initiation and progression of cancer (Ruijtenberg and van den Heuvel, 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Ruijtenberg and van den Heuvel, 2016, which discusses the role of differentiation in cancer.

claim: The expansion of lesioned clones was amplified when the TEC niche was at its sparsest.
source: Surprisingly, the expansion of lesioned clones was amplified when the TEC niche was at its sparsest – a result opposite to the non-lesioned clones which instead profit from a dense TEC niche (Figure 4—figure supplement 5).
evidence: The claim is supported by the text description and reference to Figure 4—figure supplement 5, which shows the simulation results.

claim: While non-lesioned clones gained 2 rounds of division with an increase in TEC density, lesioned clones lost 2 rounds of division.
source: While non-lesioned clones gained 2 rounds of division with an increase in TEC density, lesioned clones lost 2 rounds of division.
evidence: The claim is supported by the text description of the simulation results.

claim: Parameter combinations with reduced density and size of TECs were overrepresented in the scenarios that most increased proliferation.

evidence: The claim is supported by the text description and reference to Figure 4—figure supplement 6A–C, which shows the simulation results.

claim: In the most extreme scenario, IL7RHI or IL7RDA clones underwent up to 18 rounds of cell division – far above the 12 rounds predicted from modifying each group of parameters in isolation.

evidence: The claim is supported by the text description and reference to Figure 4—figure supplements 2–5, which show the simulation results.

claim: A defective niche amplifies the effect of other pro-proliferative modulations such as slower differentiation and shorter cell cycle, conferring a synergistic advantage to IL7RHI and IL7RDA clones compared to their normal counterparts.
source: This result suggests that a defective niche amplifies the effect of other pro-proliferative modulations such as slower differentiation and shorter cell cycle, conferring a synergistic advantage to IL7RHI and IL7RDA clones compared to their normal counterparts.
evidence: The claim is based on an inference from the simulation results.

claim: At 18 rounds of division, lesioned clones were so massive that the total lesioned cell volume was over a 1000-fold larger than the volume of the simulated organ slice.

evidence: The claim is supported by the text description and reference to Figure 4—figure supplement 6D, which shows the simulation results.

claim: In the homeostatic condition, the total volume occupied by both thymocytes and TECs amounted to only 0.7-fold of the available tissue volume.
source: In comparison, in the homeostatic condition, the total volume occupied by both thymocytes and TECs amounted to only 0.7-fold of the available tissue volume.

claim: Similar conditions in vivo would lead to thymus hyperplasia.

claim: Identifying a sparse TEC network as a new factor that could influence the clonal expansion of lesioned clones was an unexpected outcome.
source: Identifying a sparse TEC network as a new factor that could influence the clonal expansion of lesioned clones was an unexpected outcome.

evidence: The claim is based on an observation from the simulation results.

source: Conversely, we observed that a denser TEC network – characterized by a higher density of TECs with more protrusions and larger size – positively influenced the population size of non-lesioned cells but had a negative impact on the IL7RHI and IL7RDA lesioned clones (Figure 4—figure supplement 5).

claim: In conditions of high cell crowding, lack of contact with TECs put non-lesioned clones at a disadvantage, while lesioned clones appeared to benefit.

evidence: The claim is supported by the text description and reference to Figure 4—figure supplement 2 and Figure 4—video 2, which show the simulation results.

claim: In the model, if the NOTCH1 receptor fails to engage with DLL4 on TECs due to their low density or cell crowding effects, cells will remain in an undifferentiated state for a longer time.
source: In the model, if the NOTCH1 receptor fails to engage with DLL4 on TECs due to their low density or cell crowding effects, cells will remain in an undifferentiated state for a longer time.

source: A closer inspection of time-normalized clones in scenario 6 (very sparse TECs) and in scenario 26 (very dense TECs) indeed confirms that the thymocyte population has a longer turnover time when TECs are sparse (almost 80 hr, Figure 2D, middle panel) and a shorter turnover when TECs are dense (less than 60 hr, Figure 2D, right panel), indicative of the effect of Notch signaling.

claim: Cells in an environment with fewer TECs and thus lower Notch signaling will experience a prolonged proliferative phase but still require pro-proliferative signals to commit to the cell cycle.
source: Together, cells in an environment with fewer TECs and thus lower Notch signaling will experience a prolonged proliferative phase but still require pro-proliferative signals to commit to the cell cycle.
evidence: The claim is based on an inference from the simulation results and model implementation.

claim: Owing to the higher levels of IL7R signal intrinsic to the lesion, lesioned clones will be more easily competent to proliferate even without Notch signaling and, therefore, benefit from a lower TEC density.
source: Owing to the higher levels of IL7R signal intrinsic to the lesion, lesioned clones will be more easily competent to proliferate even without Notch signaling and, therefore, benefit from a lower TEC density.
evidence: The claim is based on an inference from the simulation results and model implementation.

claim: NOTCH1 signaling promotes proliferation and accelerates differentiation, while differentiation inhibits proliferation by preventing further entry into the cell cycle.
source: Thus, NOTCH1 has a dual effect in thymocytes, which we implemented in our model as an incoherent feed-forward loop (Figure 5A): NOTCH1 signaling promotes proliferation and accelerates differentiation, while differentiation inhibits proliferation by preventing further entry into the cell cycle.

claim: IL7R signaling promotes proliferation independently of NOTCH1 and has no direct or indirect effect on the differentiation process.
source: IL7R signaling promotes proliferation independently of NOTCH1 and has no direct or indirect effect on the differentiation process.

claim: Lesions that specifically delay differentiation led to higher proliferation.

evidence: The claim is supported by the text description of the simulation results.

claim: Combining delayed differentiation with IL7RDA or IL7RHI doubled proliferation.
source: Indeed, the addition of NOTCH1DA modification to IL7RDA or IL7RHI lesioned clones did not show any effect on clonal expansion, but combining delayed differentiation with IL7RDA or IL7RHI doubled proliferation.
evidence: The claim is supported by the text description of the simulation results.

claim: Modulating the effect of NOTCH1 globally does not affect proliferation in the model, which is likely due to feedback inhibition.
source: This result indicates that modulating the effect of NOTCH1 globally does not affect proliferation in our model, which is likely due to feedback inhibition, but specifically targeting the differentiation process leads to clonal expansion.
evidence: The claim is based on an inference from the simulation results.

claim: Specifically targeting the differentiation process leads to clonal expansion.
source: This result indicates that modulating the effect of NOTCH1 globally does not affect proliferation in our model, which is likely due to feedback inhibition, but specifically targeting the differentiation process leads to clonal expansion.
evidence: The claim is based on an inference from the simulation results.

claim: None of the embryos injected with the NICD∆PEST construct (N=32) displayed thymus hyperplasia at 11 dpf.
source: None of the embryos injected with the NICD∆PEST construct (N=32) displayed thymus hyperplasia at 11 dpf (Figure 5E), supporting our simulation outcome showing that global activation of NOTCH1 signaling in thymocytes alone is insufficient to result in clonal expansion within a short time frame of 8 days.

claim: 25% of injected embryos with NICD∆PEST and mycn (N=36) displayed thymus hyperplasia at 11 dpf.
source: Consequently, we observed that 25% of injected embryos with NICD∆PEST and mycn (N=36) displayed thymus hyperplasia at 11 dpf (Figure 5E).

source: Among them, 8% also exhibited a massive infiltration of GFP-expressing cells in other organs such as the brain and gut.

claim: MYCN could enact the proliferative effect of NOTCH1, shifting the balance in the incoherent feed-forward loop toward proliferation.
source: Together with our experimental results, it is therefore likely that MYCN could enact the proliferative effect of NOTCH1, shifting the balance in the incoherent feed-forward loop toward proliferation.
evidence: The claim is based on an inference from the experimental results and established knowledge.

claim: Transformed thymocytes acquire the ability to release IL-7.

evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data and reference to Figure 5—figure supplement 1B and C.

claim: Thymus hyperplasia was found in 26% (N=49) of embryos when only il7r was overexpressed in thymocytes.
source: Thymus hyperplasia was found in a slightly higher frequency of 26% (N=49) or 59% (N=29) of embryos, respectively, when only il7r or il7rNPC was overexpressed in thymocytes.

claim: Thymus hyperplasia was found in 59% (N=29) of embryos when il7rNPC was overexpressed in thymocytes.
source: Thymus hyperplasia was found in a slightly higher frequency of 26% (N=49) or 59% (N=29) of embryos, respectively, when only il7r or il7rNPC was overexpressed in thymocytes.

source: The prediction that higher NOTCH1 signaling does not lead to increased proliferation is likely due to the incoherent feed-forward loop downstream of NOTCH1, which shuts down excessive proliferation by triggering differentiation to a nondividing cell fate (Figure 5B).

source: In contrast, combining NOTCH1 with its downstream pro-proliferative effector mycn led to thymus hyperplasia.

source: However, dual activation of IL7R and the NOTCH1-MYCN axis can promote clonal expansion in vivo, leading to the rapid development of thymus hyperplasia and T-ALL in the medaka model system within 8 days.

source: The frequency of thymus hyperplasia was increased to 41% (N=32) when DNA constructs designed to overexpress il7 in TECs were co-injected with the construct overexpressing il7r in thymocytes (Figure 6B).
